items.title: November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away - NASA Science
paragraphs: NASA's Voyager mission took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. The twin spacecraft revealed details about Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune – using each planet's gravity to send them on to the next destination. Voyager set the stage for such ambitious orbiter missions as Galileo to Jupiter and Cassini to Saturn. Today both Voyager spacecraft continue to return valuable science from the far reaches of our solar system.NASA/JPL-Caltech
Twin Travelers

In 1977, NASA launched twin spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2, taking advantage of a once-every-175-year planetary alignment of the four largest planets in our solar system: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Using six gravity assists between them, this Grand Tour gave us up-close views of the gas and ice giants, including several moons. By the 1980s, the two probes went their separate ways at Saturn. As Voyager 2 continued toward Uranus and Neptune, Voyager 1 grabbed one more portrait of the solar system (excluding Mercury and Mars), including a final image of the pale blue dot we call home.
The Golden Record CoverNASA/JPL-Caltech
Playlist
“Hello from the children of planet Earth.”

Every good road trip needs some music to match. In this case, each craft carries the Golden Record, a 12-inch phonograph record with spoken greetings in 55 languages, 27 musical tracks, 116 images, and other sounds from Earth. Each record is protected by an outer cover featuring etchings showing our Sun's location relative to 14 pulsars, along with instructions on how to play it. The design used various metals to protect the information encoded from space radiation: the record used copper and gold plating, and the cover used aluminum. The cover was electroplated with an ultra-pure sample of the isotope uranium-238. Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.468 billion years.
Are We There Yet?

Did you know that a light-minute is a measure of distance, not time? In August 2012 and November 2018, Voyager 1 and 2 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun’s solar wind meets the interstellar medium. Using NASA’s Deep Space Network, Earth communicates with both spacecraft and tracks each on its journey. At the time of this article, the Canberra antenna tracked Voyager 1 at 25.80 billion km, or just over 16 billion miles.
This graphic shows the position of NASA's Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes, outside of the heliosphere, a protective bubble created by the Sun that extends well past the orbit of Pluto.NASA/JPL-Caltech

On November 18, 2026, 49 years after its launch, Voyager 1 will cross the one-light-day mark, 16.1 billion miles from the Sun. You may have heard the term light-year in your favorite sci-fi movie or show, or when stargazing and referring to an object outside of our solar system. This video best demonstrates the different distances between the inner solar system, outer solar system, and beyond, using light measurements. Additionally, track each Voyager spacecraft here.

You can get a real understanding of what a gravity assist might be like with our Gravity Assist activity and learn what it’s like to measure a “light minute” with our Measuring a Kid Minute activity guide!

items.title: MIT engineers create nanoparticles for delivering personalized cancer vaccines
items.subtitle: The particles carry a customized dose of cancer antigens that can provoke a strong immune response against tumors.
items.author: Anne Trafton | MIT News
paragraphs: A nanoscale particle with a unique structure, developed at MIT, holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines.

The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens. By precisely controlling the density of those cancer proteins, the researchers found that they could create a vaccine that prevents the development of colon tumors in mice.
This type of delivery particle could be adapted to carry many different antigens, allowing for the creation of personalized vaccines to treat individual patients’ tumors, the researchers say.

“The great thing about this is that it’s modular and we could switch out different antigens on demand, so you could design it to be patient-specific and target a known antigen for a particular kind of cancer,” says Angela Belcher, the James Mason Crafts Professor of Biological Engineering and Materials Science and Engineering and a member of the Koch Institute.

Belcher is the senior author of the study, which appears today in the journal Advanced Healthcare Materials. Shengnan Huang, research scientist at the Koch Institute, is the paper’s lead author. Jack Rudrum, Huaiyao Peng, and Hao Nghi Luu, graduate students at the Koch Institute, are also authors of the paper.
Viral vaccine assembly

For more than 20 years, Belcher’s lab has been deploying the M13 bacteriophage in a variety of applications. This virus, which is harmless to humans, consists of a single strand of DNA coated in a protein shell, or capsid.

Belcher has previously developed techniques for generating materials by engineering these viruses to self-assemble into nanoscale scaffolds. By coating these scaffolds with inorganic materials, they can create functional devices such as batteries, semiconductors, solar cells, and catalysts, with precise control over the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of the materials.
More recently, Belcher’s lab has been developing methods to control features of the phage that could allow it to be repurposed for medical applications, including vaccine delivery.

“We’re taking this toolkit that we’ve worked on and developed over decades and formatting it to be specific for vaccine therapeutics,” Belcher says. “Some of the lessons learned from making batteries and all these other things are now being fine-tuned to make personalized vaccines.”

The capsid that surrounds the M13 phage forms a long filament made from viral proteins. To create vaccines, the researchers modify one of these proteins, known as pVIII, by attaching an antigen to the end of the protein. This can be done by adding the gene for the antigen to the virus’s DNA.

Some of the lab’s previous work had suggested that changing the density of cancer antigens attached to the capsid could affect the strength of the resulting immune response. In the new study, Huang wanted to find a way to control that density.

“The antigen is the specific target we want to initiate the immune response against, which means we have to ensure the right dose of antigen to make sure that we can have a strong immune response,” she says.

Huang discovered that she could increase the density of the modified pVIII proteins by adding one or two negatively charged amino acids to the protein sequence. The density could be further fine-tuned by adding a genetic mutation that slows down production of the antigen protein.

In this study, the researchers also figured out how to boost the phage’s own ability to act as a vaccine adjuvant, by changing the genetic sequence of the virus’s DNA. Most vaccines need to be delivered along with an adjuvant such as aluminum hydroxide, which helps to stimulate a strong immune response. However, the M13 phage can act as an adjuvant itself because single-stranded DNA activates a pathway called TLR9, which is part of the body’s innate immune system.

“We can control the exact length. We can control the exact antigen expression, density, pattern, the exact adjuvant amount. A lot of times with a vaccine, you’ll have to put a different adjuvant with it, but now it’s all genetically encoded,” Belcher says.
Targeting tumors

Using these techniques, the researchers showed that they could design phages that express an antigen called SIINFEKL at densities ranging from 6 percent to 70 percent. SIINFEKL, a small protein that can be engineered into tumors, is often used as a model to test vaccine effectiveness.
The researchers tested two of these vaccines in mice, one with 6 percent density and one with 35 percent, and found that the one with 35 percent was the most protective.

After vaccination with the higher-density particles, mice were much less likely to develop tumors when later exposed to melanoma cancer cells expressing the SIINFEKL antigen. These mice also generated more T cells targeting SIINFEKL. This is, in part, because dendritic cells, which help to activate T cells, were more likely to take up vaccines with higher antigen density, the researchers found.

In another set of experiments, the researchers created and tested a vaccine carrying a neoantigen, which is only present in the tumor cells. This protein, known as ADPGK, is specifically expressed by colon tumors in a mouse model of cancer. When given the higher density vaccine, these mice were much less likely to develop colon tumors.

In this study, the researchers tested the vaccine as a way to prevent cancer from developing, and in their previous work, they adapted it for use to treat mouse colon tumors that have already formed. In the future, they also hope to use it to combat other types of cancer.

“This interesting work adds another cog to improve the translational potential of the M13 phage platform for cancer immunotherapeutics,” says Alberto Danielli, an associate professor of molecular biology at the University of Bologna, who was not involved in the study. “I look forward to seeing whether this platform is also effective against established tumors and whether additional tumor antigens can be displayed with comparable molecular and immunological efficacy.”
This platform could be especially well-suited for personalized cancer vaccines, because many different antigens could be swapped into the vaccine.

“Because this is a modularly engineered platform, we can change the antigen we are interested in. For colon cancer, we use this specific antigen. For other types of cancer, we can just plug in other antigens and they can be assembled in this platform,” Huang says.
The research was funded, in part, by the Koch Institute Frontier Research Program, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.

items.title: APOD: 2026 October 30 – Haunting the Cepheus Flare - NASA Science
paragraphs: APOD
Astronomy Picture of the Day
Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Haunting the Cepheus Flare

Explanation: Spooky shapes seem to haunt this dusty expanse, drifting through the night in the royal constellation Cepheus. Of course, the shapes are cosmic dust clouds visible in dimly reflected starlight. Far from your own neighborhood, they lurk above the plane of the Milky Way at the edge of the Cepheus Flare molecular cloud complex some 1,200 light-years away. Over 2 light-years across and brighter than most of the other ghostly apparitions, vdB 141 or Sh2-136 is also known as the Ghost Nebula. It lies at lower right in the starry field of view. Inside the Ghost Nebula are reddish telltale signs of dense cores collapsing in the early stages of star formation. With the eerie hue of interstellar dust reflecting bluish light from hot young stars of NGC 7023, the Iris Nebula stands out against the dark just left of center. In the broad telescopic frame, these fertile interstellar dust fields stretch almost six full moons across the sky.Tomorrow's picture: night on a spooky planet

items.title: Vega Island Frozen in Fright - NASA Science
paragraphs: March 22, 2025
October 10, 2026
Part of an ice-covered Antarctic island has the appearance of a grinning skull in profile, with a rock outcrop as an eye socket and lateral moraine as a mouth.NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin

Part of an ice-covered Antarctic island has the appearance of a grinning skull in profile. Some of the face has a gray appearance where seasonal snow is gone and bare ice is exposed.NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin
Part of an ice-covered Antarctic island has the appearance of a grinning skull in profile, with a rock outcrop as an eye socket and lateral moraine as a mouth.NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin

Part of an ice-covered Antarctic island has the appearance of a grinning skull in profile. Some of the face has a gray appearance where seasonal snow is gone and bare ice is exposed.NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin
March 22, 2025
October 10, 2026

Shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, Vega Island is an eerie sight to behold. On this speck of land east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ice, rock outcrops, and glacial moraines combine to create the appearance of a smirking skull in profile looking toward Devil Island.

These images show Vega Island’s creepy countenance at the start of austral autumn (left) and in spring (right). They were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.) A nunatak jutting out of the ice has the appearance of an eye socket, a lateral moraine forms a mouth, and Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier constitutes a jawbone. In the March 2025 image, a layer of snow coats the ice, which is typical of the region’s wettest month. That contrasts with the October 2026 image, when snow is absent from large areas and darker ice surfaces are visible.

Above-average temperatures in winter 2026—particularly in June—were partly responsible for so much bare ice in October, said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The ice exposed on Vega and nearby islands indicates limited new snow accumulation over the winter, further reduced by sublimation and wind scouring, he said. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”

The melt season ahead may also be more trick than treat. Satellite images acquired in recent decades show ice loss from other glaciers on the island as well, with increased areas of exposed bedrock.

items.title: Map Showing Potential Origins of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001 - NASA Science
paragraphs: Downloads
Map Showing Potential Origins of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001
JPEG (1.22 MB)
Description

This global map of Mars shows 13 locations that match the mineralogy and chemistry of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. While scientists can never know for sure where a Martian meteorite originated, Teghaza 001 includes clues that link it to highlands in the southern hemisphere of the Red Planet.

The base map of this image was produced with data from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter instrument aboard NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor mission. Scientists used data from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter to identify areas of the map (noted with white circles) that have similar mineralogy and chemistry as Teghaza 001.

Slice of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001

PIA26801 Figure A
TIFF (26.10 MB)
Description

This slice of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth, was used to determine the age of the rock. Reflected light images like these serve as a scientist’s road map, helping them find minerals of interest to analyze by different instruments.
Figure A

Figure A is the same image with annotations showing minerals like iron-titanium oxides (brighter grains) and pyroxene (medium gray), both of which tell a story about the formation of Mars’ crust and mantle. Shocked plagioclase (darker gray) is created by extreme pressures during impacts, including the one that sent Teghaza 001 flying through space to Earth. The alteration represents fine grain carbonate, sulfate and clay minerals formed on Earth.

items.title: Halloween Aboard the International Space Station - NASA
paragraphs: Although no ghouls, goblins, or trick-or-treaters come knocking at the International Space Station’s front hatch, crew members aboard the orbiting laboratory still like to get in the Halloween spirit. Whether individually or as an entire crew, they dress up in sometimes spooky, sometimes scary, but always creative costumes, often designed from materials available aboard the space station.
Take a look at how the station crews have celebrated in years past.
ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano finally gets his wish to fly like Superman aboard the International Space Station during Expedition 37.
A trio of Expedition 73 astronauts dressed for Halloween in 2025.

Expedition 70 astronauts Jasmin Moghbeli of NASA, left, Satoshi Furukawa of JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), NASA astronaut Loral O’Hara, and ESA astronaut Andreas Mogensen celebrate Halloween 2023.

In 2022, Expedition 68 astronauts Koichi Wakata of JAXA, left, and NASA astronauts Francisco “Frank” Rubio, Nicole Mann, and Josh Cassada dressed as popular video game and cartoon characters, using stowage containers in their Halloween costumes and holding improvised trick-or-treat bags.
Expedition 66 crewmembers NASA astronaut Shane Kimbrough, left, Thomas Pesquet of ESA, Akihiko Hoshide of JAXA, and NASA astronaut Mark Vande Hei show off their Halloween cards.
Members of Expedition 61, NASA astronaut Christina Koch, top left, ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano, and NASA astronauts Andrew “Drew” Morgan, and Jessica Meir, show off their Halloween spirit in 2019.

Flight Engineer Sergei Prokopyev of Roscosmos, dressed as Elvis Presley, Commander Alexander Gerst of ESA as Darth Vader, and Flight Engineer Serena Auñón-Chancellor of NASA as a mad scientist, pose for a Halloween photo inside the Kibo Japanese Experiment Module pressurized module aboard the space station during Expedition 57.NASA
In 2017, Expedition 53 crew members show off their Halloween costumes.
Expedition 21 NASA astronaut Nicole Stott shows off her Halloween costume.
For Halloween 2009, the Expedition 21 crew shows off its costumes.
Follow the astronauts aboard the space station to see how they celebrate holidays in space.
The space station remains a vital scientific platform, providing the foundation needed to survive and thrive as humanity ventures into the unexplored territories of our universe.

items.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found - NASA
paragraphs: Called Teghaza 001, this rose-colored rock is one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. Credit: © Darryl Pitt / Maine Mineral & Gem Museum

When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found. Named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, the meteorite is one of roughly 435 from the Red Planet.

In a paper published Thursday in Science, researchers offered an initial characterization of Teghaza 001, providing a rare snapshot of Mars’ ancient crust and formation. What scientists learn from future studies could help answer many questions, including how water and rocks interacted on ancient Mars. A separate paper published in Science Advances in June detailed the meteorite’s water content, offering a look at how water shaped the early planet’s surface.

“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” said the paper’s lead author, Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars.”
This slice of Teghaza 001, a Martian meteorite, was used to study its mineralogy and chemistry. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
Rose-colored stone

What sets Teghaza 001 apart from other Martian meteorites is its texture and age as well as the uniqueness of its igneous, or volcanic, minerals. It is one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth. While invaluable, the others provide more limited glimpses of Mars’ geological history. They include ALH84001, which is composed almost entirely of one mineral and is similar in age to Teghaza 001. The other meteorite, nicknamed “Black Beauty,” formed about 2.1 billion years ago and is composed of small, volcanic rock fragments.

Unlike its ancient peers, Teghaza 001 has a mix of igneous minerals that tells a story about how the planet’s crust formed from cooling magma before it was eventually altered by subsurface water. The meteorite’s distinctive mineralogy matches what NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has observed in the planet’s cratered southern highlands. No one will ever know exactly where the meteorite originated on Mars, but the paper identifies several potential locations that match Teghaza 001’s mineralogy and chemistry.

“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” said the new paper’s second author, Lee Saper, who conducted the research while at JPL as a postdoctoral scholar. Lee now is a scientist at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley. “It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water.”

Although the Mars meteorites found on Earth differ from one another, they share a common history, having been blasted off the Red Planet’s surface by an impact, followed by a trajectory that eventually placed them on Earth and into the hands of scientists. Meteorites are often found by collectors in deserts or snowy plains, where they stand out from the rest of the barren landscape. Scientists can verify a meteorite as Martian by matching its mineral and chemical components to data collected by NASA’s Mars missions, including the Viking landers as well as the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.
Scientists identified 13 locations on Mars that match the mineralogy and chemistry of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/USGS
Signs of water
When Liu was first asked to look at Teghaza 001, she almost passed on the opportunity.

Researchers at the University of New Mexico had already identified it as Martian based on its oxygen isotopes, which serve as geochemical fingerprints for different planetary bodies. In this case, the researchers matched the meteorite’s oxygen isotopes to those seen in other Martian meteorites. Teghaza 001 appeared to be a shergottite which is the most common class of meteorite from the Red Planet. As an expert in planetary samples, Liu has seen plenty of those, but she decided to take a peek, anyway.

At the very least, there were odd textures and unusual minerals she hadn’t seen before. Liu and her colleagues discovered zircon crystals in Teghaza 001, which record clues to a rock’s formation and can be used by geologists to precisely age-date a sample. Further analysis revealed when Teghaza 001 formed and when certain changes, like water alteration, occurred.

Caltech coauthor Francois Tissot helped the researchers utilize a novel age-dating method pioneered by his team. Compared with bulk-analysis techniques, where a sample is entirely dissolved and analyzed, Tissot’s in-situ rubidium-strontium age-dating used a piece of Teghaza 001 that was smaller than a fingernail, analyzing single mineral grains on its surface. Besides its extreme precision and speed, the technique preserves rare samples like Martian meteorites for future studies.

“Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite,” Tissot said. “Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from other planets, their moons, and asteroids.”

When the age-dating results came back, Liu was shocked: This rock had been altered by Martian water sometime around 4.1 billion years ago, suggesting it originally formed even earlier. Clues within the oxygen isotopes, texture, and chemistry of Teghaza 001 minerals point to a much more dynamic water cycle on early Mars.
This year’s papers are just the start. Liu and her co-authors are eager to see what the rest of the scientific community can learn from Teghaza 001.
“We’ve only scratched the surface,” Liu said.
-end-
Andrew GoodJet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif.818-393-2433andrew.c.good@jpl.nasa.gov

items.title: Next Haunt: A scary “problem set” in the basement of Next House
items.subtitle: For more than a decade, MIT students have turned Next House’s basement into a spooky escape-room style test of puzzles, teamwork, and ingenuity.
items.author: Sarah Foote | Division of Student Life
paragraphs: You know it’s autumn when the scent of pumpkin spice latte begins to waft through the air at the Dunkin’ in the Stratton Student Center, and students in MIT’s Next House residence hall diligently begin to piece together the many parts needed to showcase Next Haunt — a combination of a Halloween haunted house and escape room, built in the basement of the hall.

Every fall since 2014, students — also known as hauntmasters — spend several weekends building the room and preparing puzzles, physical tasks, or word challenges to obtain a code to open locks that let participants escape the house. This year’s theme, titled “Where the Light Ends,” follows “Terror Under Destruction,” “Next Stop: MBTA,” and last year’s theme: “Get in the HOLE.”

Next Haunt is free and open to all MIT students, also known as “test subjects.” Participants typically spend around 20 minutes in small, dark, enclosed rooms, working with four to six teammates to find the clues they need to escape.

Along the way, they have to navigate zombies — played by student actors — who may shout at them or splash them with blood (fake) while they solve the puzzles. If a zombie touches a participant, they become “paralyzed” and can no longer move, but they can still communicate and relay information to their teammates.

Teams must work closely, strategize, delegate tasks, and communicate effectively as the clock counts down. The group with the quickest escape time gets bragging rights, and every group signs their names on a wooden board to show that they participated.

MIT junior Kiyoko Hayano, Next Haunt co-producer, says, “I became involved in Next Haunt during my first semester at MIT because I had experience with larger-scale painting. I split the build director’s role with two other freshmen, including Michelle Liang, our current assistant producer. I thought this would be a great opportunity to take a break from psets and work with my hands, and fell in love with the club.”
Safety first

Before the room is built and the puzzles and costumes are created, careful planning takes place to ensure the escape room is safe, fire-resistant, and passes an on-site inspection. MIT’s Campus Construction and Environment, Health, and Safety offices are involved from the start, and all students who partake in the build are required to attend safety orientation and tool training.

“We currently have 18 people on our executive team, and we have 12 outside volunteers come help over the first few weekends of Next Haunt build,” says Hayano. “We then run Next Haunt for six-and-a-half hours every night for two weekends at the end of October.”

Once the build is complete, several alumni volunteers conduct a “test run” to make sure the puzzles and clues are hard, but not impossible, and anyone who wants to leave the room before the allotted time can easily find the door out built with Velcro closures.

Escaping by solving the puzzles is not easy, and not all participants are successful. Last year, only 16 percent of the 73 teams successfully got out of the room. The winning team escaped in just under 15 minutes.

Alumnus and previous Next Haunt producer Allen Lin ’26 notes, “I became involved with Next Haunt in my freshman year after being a test subject myself, and I loved the creative and building process so much I wanted to join. If a zombie touches a participant, they become “paralyzed” and can no longer move, but they can still communicate and relay information to their teammates.

items.title: Magnetic sensors track muscle movement, for better prosthetic limb control
items.subtitle: Researchers hope to use these sensors to help people with amputation achieve more natural movements with their prosthetic limbs.
items.author: Anne Trafton | MIT News
paragraphs: MIT researchers have shown that they can accurately track muscle movement using tiny magnetic beads implanted in the muscle. These measurements could make it easier for people with certain types of amputations to control their prosthetic limbs.

For decades, researchers have been working to develop neuroprosthetic limbs, which use neural information from muscles remaining after an amputation to guide the prosthetic limb. Measurements of a muscle’s length, velocity and activation can be fed into the control algorithms that guide the limbs, allowing individuals with leg amputation to walk with a more natural gait, or those with arm amputation to manipulate objects more effectively.

Until now, these devices have relied on muscle activity measurements from electrodes placed on the surface of the skin. However, those measurements have not proven reliable enough to ensure safety while walking with a neuroprosthetic leg.
The MIT team hopes that their new magnetic tracking system, which offers more accurate measurements, will enable commercial development of such limbs.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Researchers demonstrate how the two magnetic beads are wirelessly tracked.
Credit: Courtesy of the researchers

“For four decades, the standard methodology for neurally controlling prostheses has been to use skin electrodes to measure muscle activation. However, to control a prosthetic limb, joint position, torque, or impedance has to be controlled, and one cannot directly determine such mechanical signals using electrical activation alone,” says Hugh Herr, a professor of media arts and sciences, co-director of the K. Lisa Yang Center for Bionics at MIT, an associate member of MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, and the senior author of the new study.
In the new study, which appears today in Nature Sensors, the researchers demonstrated the accuracy of the magnetic measurements in three participants with below-knee amputations.

“This interface is minimally invasive, so it could be accessible to more people. You place two beads in the muscle and you have access to all of this rich information about the muscle dynamics,” says Christopher Shallal, an MIT graduate student in the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology and one of the lead authors of the paper.
The paper’s other lead author is Cameron Taylor PhD ’20, an assistant professor of biomedical engineering at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
Tracking muscles

For many years, Herr’s lab has been developing human-machine interfaces that can be used to control an artificial limb in a way that makes it more like using a natural limb. Obtaining accurate measurements of how the user is moving the muscles at the amputation site is critical to the success of this type of prosthesis.

Electrodes on the surface of the skin can reveal the electrical activation of the muscle below, and those measurements can be converted to estimates of how much a muscle is contracting or flexing. Based on that input, a robotic controller generates commands that guide the prosthetic limb in the user’s intended direction.

However, that measurement approach, known as electromyography, does not always provide accurate enough information. The electrical signal is not a perfect proxy for muscle dynamics; for example, when a muscle is held at a fixed length for several seconds, the signal fades. Additionally, the electrodes may pick up signals from muscles other than the intended target, and sweat can interfere with detection of the signal.

Last year, Herr and his colleagues reported a “bionic knee” prosthesis that uses electrodes implanted in the muscles to provide accurate measurements and feed them into a robotic controller. This approach proved successful in a small clinical study, but alongside that work, Herr’s team has also been working on a less invasive approach that relies on magnets instead of electrodes.

With this approach, known as magnetomicrometry, pairs of magnets are implanted into muscles. When a muscle contracts or stretches, external sensors placed on the skin can measure the change in distance between the magnets, allowing muscle length and velocity to be calculated.

“Magnets can be tracked wirelessly through the body, so you can get very specific muscle signals and measure the mechanical output of the muscle without needing to be extremely invasive,” Shallal says.
Better control

In a 2021 study led by Taylor, Herr’s lab first demonstrated the magnet-based technique in animal models. The new Nature Sensors study extends the approach to humans with long-term magnetic implants. For the study, the researchers recruited three participants who have below-knee amputations.

All of these participants had a type of amputation that creates what’s called an agonist-antagonist myoneural interface (AMI). With this surgical procedure, muscle pairs are reconnected during surgery so that they still dynamically communicate with each other within the residual limb. This sensory feedback, called proprioception, helps the wearer of the prosthesis to decide how to position and move their prosthetic limb.

Participants had magnets implanted in up to four muscles of the ankle joint. The surgeries were performed at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in collaboration with plastic surgeon Matthew Carty, a co-author of the study. The beads are 3 millimeters in diameter, about the size of a sesame seed. The magnets are made from an alloy of neodymium, iron, and boron, and are coated with gold and a polymer called parylene C to make them biocompatible. The magnetic signals can be read from a depth of up to 6 centimeters from the skin’s surface, using a customized external sensor that is worn over the skin, positioned over the muscles that are being tracked.

Each of the participants in this study also had electrodes implanted into the same muscles that received magnetic beads. This allowed the researchers to compare the accuracy of three different types of measurements: magnetomicrometry, electromyography with implanted electrodes, and electromyography with electrodes on the surface of the skin.

During the experiments, the participants were not wearing a prosthetic limb but were asked to perform tasks such as moving a cursor on a screen to a particular target using their muscle movements. Using each of the three measurement techniques, the signals generated by the muscle movements were translated into control signals that, in this case, moved the cursor but in the future could be fed into the controller of a robotic ankle-foot prosthesis.

“The cursor on the screen represented the degrees of freedom that they would control on a robotic ankle-foot prosthesis. This virtual neuroprosthetic task allowed us to compare the performance across different neural interfaces, and our results suggest that the magnet-based approach can offer more accurate and stable control,” Shallal says.
The researchers are now performing a larger study in which they are evaluating how well people can control prosthetic limbs using measurements from the magnetic beads.
The research was funded, in part, by the Yang Tan Collective at MIT as well as a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship and an MIT HEALS Graduate Fellowship.

items.title: New system gives users more control over their online experience
items.subtitle: The Social.Wiki framework enables anyone to easily edit social websites within the system, while allowing them to choose the content they see.
items.author: Adam Zewe | MIT News
paragraphs: A user who is frustrated with changes a social media company made to their favorite messaging platform, like the introduction of an annoying AI chatbot, can’t do much to address the situation, short of leaving the platform.
Now, MIT researchers are offering an alternative path.
They’ve created Social.Wiki, a system that allows users to easily edit any social application made within Social.Wiki, and choose which of the edits made by others they want to see.

For example, a user could change a messaging site on Social.Wiki to remove an AI chatbot and instead add a restaurant voting feature so their group chat can finally decide where they are going out for dinner.

“The infrastructure that we are all dependent on online is very rigid. It is based on these one-size-fits-all applications that we don’t have a lot of power to change. This project is about trying to imagine what a different web would look like where anyone can participate,” says Theia Henderson, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student, and lead author of a new paper on Social.Wiki.
The researchers envision a world in which, if a user is unhappy with their social app, they can edit it to change it however they like — without getting cut off from their social connections.
Play video

The platform enables users with no coding expertise to create a range of websites, including social sites like photo sharing networks, discussion forums, and dating apps. It handles all back-end work, eliminating the need for creators to set up servers or arrange databases.

Social.Wiki employs a decentralized infrastructure that allows users to retain ownership of their data as they create, edit, and navigate social websites within the platform. It also includes a “data guard” that protects user data from malicious or buggy applications.

Through case studies and user tests, the researchers demonstrated the breadth of applications people can create with Social.Wiki, including a rideshare app where riders propose the prices they are willing to pay and a collaborative canvas for creating art together.
While Social.Wiki is still in its early days, the researchers plan to continue refining the platform as they deploy it to a wider audience.

“We want to empower the creation of far more social applications that meet the needs of unusual small groups. Each group is unusual, but everyone is in unusual groups. Everybody has their own needs for social applications that we want to be able to address,” says David Karger, professor of EECS, a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), and senior author of the paper.

Henderson and Karger are joined on the paper by EECS graduate students Carmel Schare and Ana Dodik; Clemens Klokmose, a professor of computer science at Aarhus University in Denmark; Ziv Epstein, a postdoc in the MIT Media Lab; and David D. Clark, an MIT research scientist. The paper will be presented at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in November.
Letting users choose

Social.Wiki is a Wikipedia-like system in which users can navigate to different web applications or create their own web application within the Social.Wiki ecosystem. Each website has an “edit” button that allows any user to change the content of the site, from the text color on a message board to the pricing algorithm in a ride-sharing app.
Clicking the “edit” button in Social.Wiki opens a page that lets users view and edit the source code manually or prompt an AI assistant to make changes to the site.
This platform builds on the researchers’ prior work on Graffiti, a web framework with a decentralized infrastructure that makes building personalized applications easier.

With Social.Wiki, the researchers sought a collaboratively editable system that would allow anyone to revise web applications to be ideally suited for their needs and the needs of groups they belong to.

To enable this structure, Social.Wiki relies on a strategy the researchers call “plural governance.” Instead of a central moderator deciding which content users will see, each Social.Wiki user can choose the rules that determine which edits they will see on Social.Wiki webpages.
Users can also identify “trusted editors,” so they will see edits from individuals or organizations they consider reliable.

For instance, a user could customize their rules, or “governance policy,” so they only see edits to a site that have been endorsed by at least two of their friends. When the Social.Wiki browser loads a site for a user, it applies the governance policy that user selected to decide which version of the site to present.

For example, based on each user’s choices and edits, the system might show one user a ride-sharing app with a uniform pricing algorithm while another user might see the same app with a dynamic pricing algorithm.
“No website is tied to a particular machine. This means we have no centralized ownership over the websites or the underlying infrastructure,” Henderson explains.
Security and creativity
In this decentralized infrastructure, user data are stored separately from the websites that access it, which helps keep data secure.
Social.Wiki also employs a data guard, which prompts a user to review each request from a website that is attempting to access their data.
“In Social.Wiki, these websites are held in common and anybody can edit them, but the data guard makes sure that each user stays in control of what happens to their data,” Karger adds.

The researchers evaluated Social.Wiki through several case studies. For one, they developed a messaging platform that allows participants to modify the chat’s styling and interface without affecting the experience of others. In another, they built a collaborative ride-sharing app that enables riders to adjust the fare they want to pay using a transparent “living wage” calculator.
They also sponsored a hackathon in which users built Social.Wiki applications.

Participants developed a range of creative sites, including a housing co-op communication tool that organizes chats on a map of the co-op, as well as a garden-themed microblogging site where posts are “planted” as flowers.

“Even the little bit that has been done so far with Social.Wiki demonstrates that there is so much more that could be done with social apps if users could specialize them to meet a particular group’s needs,” Karger says.

Moving forward, the researchers are working to deploy Social.Wiki to a broader audience and gather feedback from more diverse user groups. They also want to make technical upgrades to enable end-to-end encryption on private message data and provide better developer tools.
This work was funded, in part, by Schmidt Sciences and the National Science Foundation (NSF).

items.title: Caltech Names Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman as NASA JPL Deputy - NASA
paragraphs: Former NASA astronaut and Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman joins Caltech and NASA JPL as Caltech associate vice president and JPL deputy director on Nov. 30. Photo Credit: NASA

Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on Nov. 30, 2026.

“Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “As commander of Artemis II, he helped carry America back around the Moon, and now, as an emeritus astronaut, he will continue giving back to NASA from a new vantage point at JPL. Reid is joining a storied laboratory that has made an enormous amount of history, and there is a lot more ahead. I am excited to see what he and the JPL team accomplish in the years to come.”
During the Artemis II test flight, Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen journeyed 695,081 miles on a lunar flyby that took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before.

“It feels fitting for Reid, who with the Artemis II crew traveled farther from Earth than any human in history, to join Caltech and JPL — institutions that for nearly 90 years have sent spacecraft into the far reaches of our solar system and beyond,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director and Caltech vice president. “Reid shares our drive for discovery, knows what it takes to lead teams through high-stakes missions, and has a remarkable ability to inspire people everywhere. He adds incredible bench strength to our leadership team as we build on the lab’s legacy and shape its future together.”

After joining NASA’s astronaut corps in 2009, Wiseman went on to serve as flight engineer aboard the International Space Station for the 165-day Expedition 41 mission in 2014 and was a commander of NASA’s 21st Extreme Environment Mission Operations expedition, during which he lived for eight days in a habitat on the ocean floor in 2016. As the agency’s chief astronaut from December 2020 to November 2022, Wiseman led NASA’s astronaut corps, overseeing crew flight readiness and crew safety for all NASA human spaceflight missions. During his years of service at the agency, he has conducted hundreds of scientific experiments.

“I’ve explored the furthest reaches of what a human can explore at NASA — and there were truly no words in the English vocabulary to describe seeing the Sun disappear behind the Moon from deep space. But that experience was really the jumping off point to go do the impossible things that Caltech and JPL dream, dare together, and do for NASA and the nation,” Wiseman said. “What an awesome time in my career to join this team and to try and push humanity and push our understanding of the solar system and the universe.”

Wiseman joins JPL, NASA’s only federally funded research and development center, as the lab approaches its 90th anniversary since being founded by Caltech. In his role as Caltech’s associate vice president and JPL deputy director, Wiseman will be responsible for the strategic leadership, stewardship and continuous improvement of laboratory operations, including close partnership with Caltech on institutional planning, management and compliance. Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on Nov. 30, 2026.

“Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “As commander of Artemis II, he helped carry America back around the Moon, and now, as an emeritus astronaut, he will continue giving back to NASA from a new vantage point at JPL. During the Artemis II test flight, Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen journeyed 695,081 miles on a lunar flyby that took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before.

items.title: NASA Welcomes Vietnam as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory - NASA
paragraphs: Credit: NASA

The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.

“Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks for the ceremony. “NASA and the Vietnam National Space Center have built momentum in satellite innovation, land-use research, and radar-based Earth observation. Joining the Artemis Accords opens a new chapter in that relationship. We’ve aligned on the principles. The opportunities are in front of us, and now we can build on that foundation together. We are proud to welcome Vietnam to the Artemis Accords community.”

Vietnam’s Minister of Science and Technology Vũ Hải Quân signed the Artemis Accords on behalf of the country during the Vietnam International Digital Week in Ha Long. The United States Ambassador to Vietnam Jennifer Wicks also participated in the signing event.

Vietnam’s decision extends the U.S.-Vietnam Comprehensive Strategic Partnership into a new frontier. Built on more than 30 years of cooperation, the partnership spans defense, economic, law enforcement, war legacy, and technological cooperation, and it advances peace, stability, and prosperity in a free and open Indo-Pacific.

Earlier this year, NASA partnered with Vietnam’s Vietnamese-German University to support the agency’s Soil Moisture Active Passive mission, which measures surface-soil water worldwide. Vietnam also inaugurated its National Space Center in Hanoi and is developing domestic satellite capabilities through the LOTUSat program, focusing on Earth observation, weather monitoring, and disaster response.

In 2020, NASA and the State Department joined with seven other founding nations to establish the Artemis Accords, responding to the growing interest in lunar activities by both governments and private companies. They introduced the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing the safety and coordination between nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Signing the Artemis Accords means committing to explore peaceably and transparently, to render aid to those in need, to enable access to scientific data that all of humanity can learn from, to ensure activities do not interfere with those of others, and to preserve historically significant sites and artifacts by developing best practices for space exploration for the benefit of all.
More countries are expected to sign the Artemis Accords in the months and years ahead, as NASA continues its work to establish a safe, peaceful, and prosperous future in space.
Learn more about the Artemis Accords at:
https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-accords

items.title: Artemis III SLS Core Stage Joins Boosters at Kennedy - NASA
paragraphs: The SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is lifted from the transfer aisle of the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026.NASA/Sean Cannon
The SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is lifted from the transfer aisle of the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. NASA/Sean Cannon
The SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is horizontal in the transfer aisle of the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. NASA/Cory S Huston

The SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is integrated alongside the twin solid rocket booster motor segments on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida completing its short stack configuration. NASA/Sean Cannon

The SLS (Space Launch System) rocket core stage is integrated with the solid rocket boosters for Artemis III in High Bay 3 of the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida to complete its short stack configuration.NASA/Frank Michaux

NASA’s Artemis III SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is integrated alongside the twin solid rocket boosters on Oct. 28 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Technicians lifted the 212-foot rocket stage from the facility’s High Bay 2 using a one-of-a kind lifting beam designed to place the stage onto the mobile launcher. Once testing and checkouts are complete, teams will roll the core stage and booster stack out to Launch Pad 39B to conduct a tanking test where liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen fuel will be loaded only into the core stage and launch teams will practice countdown procedures and timelines.

The Artemis III mission will launch NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano in the Orion spacecraft on top of the SLS rocket to test rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial spacecraft from Blue Origin and SpaceX ahead of future mission to land astronauts on the Moon.
Photo credit: NASA/Sean Cannon, Cory S Huston, and Frank Michaux

items.title: Seven MIT affiliates elected to the National Academy of Medicine for 2026
items.subtitle: Professor Michael Yaffe and six MIT alumni are honored for their outstanding professional achievement and commitment to service.
items.author: Bendta Schroeder | Koch Institute
paragraphs: During its annual meeting on Oct. 19, the National Academy of Medicine (NAM) announced election of 100 new members, including MIT faculty member Michael Yaffe and six MIT alumni: Steven Allen Abrams ’79; Susan L. Ettner PhD ’91; Diane Medved Harper ’80, SM ’82; Albert Icksang Ko ’81; Jennifer Lewis ScD ’91; and Alexander Marson PhD ’08.

Election to the academy is considered one of the highest honors in the fields of health and medicine and recognizes individuals who have demonstrated outstanding professional achievement and commitment to service.

Michael Yaffe, David H. Koch (1962) Professor of Science, is the founding director of the MIT Center for Precision Cancer Medicine, as well as a professor in the MIT departments of Biology and Biological Engineering and a member of the MIT Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research. He is also an attending surgeon and intensivist at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, where he specializes in injury and surgical oncology, and was recently appointed as senior advisor to the director of the National Cancer Institute (NCI) for the NCI Intramural Research Program.

The NAM recognized Yaffe for “the discovery of phospho Ser/Thr-binding domains in proteins and how they regulate signaling pathways controlling the cell cycle or in response to stress.” His contributions in this area were pivotal to “the emergence of systems biology and bioinformatic approaches to map motifs across the kinome and characterize biochemical principles that determine kinase-substrate selectivity.”

Yaffe’s work in cell signaling more broadly seeks to understand how signaling pathways that control DNA damage responses, survival, cell cycle progression, and immune activation are integrated at the molecular and systems levels to control tumor outcomes after treatment, and to translate discoveries into more effective cancer drug combinations and treatment strategies.

Yaffe earned his doctoral degree in biophysical chemistry and his medical degree from Case Western Reserve University. Before joining the MIT faculty in 2000, he completed residencies in both general surgery at University Hospitals of Cleveland and surgical oncology at New England Deaconess Hospital, a fellowship in surgical critical care at Harvard Medical School’s Harvard-Longwood Critical Care Program, and a postdoctoral fellowship with Lewis Cantley at Harvard Medical School. Yaffe is a decorated veteran of the war in Afghanistan and retired as a colonel from the U.S. Army Reserve Medical Corps in 2021. He is also the scientific editor-in-chief of Science Signaling, an elected member of the Association of American Physicians, and a 2021 MacVicar Faculty Fellow.
MIT alumni who were elected to the NAM for 2026 are affiliated with the following departments:
Steven Allen Abrams ’79 is an alumnus of the Department of Biology.
Susan L. Ettner PhD ’91 is an alumna of the Department of Economics.
Diane Medved Harper ’80, SM ’82 is an alumna of the departments of Chemical Engineering and Materials Science and Engineering.
Albert Icksang Ko ’81 is an alumnus of the departments of Chemistry and Biology.
Jennifer Lewis ScD ’91 is an alumna of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering.
Alexander Marson PhD ’08 is an alumnus of the Department of Biology.

Established originally as the Institute of Medicine in 1970 by the National Academy of Sciences, the National Academy of Medicine addresses critical issues in health, science, medicine, and related policy, and inspires positive actions across sectors.

“I am thrilled to welcome these outstanding health and medicine leaders into the National Academy of Medicine,” said NAM President Monica M. Bertagnolli. “Their extraordinary talent and commitment to advancing evidence-based guidance and solutions for our country’s greatest health-care challenges will strengthen our efforts to improve health for all.”

items.title: NASA University Challenge Ignites Trajectory of Drone Entrepreneur
paragraphs: Four co-founders of AG3 Labs –from left Matt Atkinson, Gavin Gardner, Ryan Atkinson, and Gryson Gardner – show off the military training drones their company builds at a U.S. Army event at Camp Grayling in Michigan. As a student, Gavin was on a Michigan State team twice selected for participation in NASA’s University Student Research Challenge. His NASA experience served as a foundation for the creation of AG3. AG3 Labs

Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge.

Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students in a lab setting, he and his team were completely new to things like creating budgets, handling large sums of money, and promoting their work for crowdfunding.

That’s why demonstrating both engineering and entrepreneurship skills are major tentpoles of NASA’s University Student Research Challenge (USRC), an initiative that provides grants to teams of college students interested in helping the agency realize its aeronautical research goals.

“Half the battle is building your product,” Gardner said recently. “The other half is selling the product in a way that everyone else can understand what you’re doing and not talking in nerdy, engineering ways.”
We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers.
STEVEN HOLZ
NASA USRC Manager

Gardner and his Michigan State USRC alumni teammates are still using those lessons today, as aerospace developers. In 2024, they founded their own company, AG3 Labs, which specializes in drones for military training exercises.

“I don’t think I would discredit our technical expertise in getting us to where we are today, but I know that USRC was a booster that really amplified our trajectory at such a young age,” Gardner said.

NASA USRC manager Steven Holz said Gardner’s experience shows what students can accomplish when they receive both a grant and guidance – enabling a future workforce and contributing to the aviation industry.

“We are proud to see the success of USRC alumni,” Holz said. “We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers.”
Research path
Gardner’s path to running his own company began with a middle school age trip to Space Camp, where he began realizing that he wanted to be an engineer.
The engineering bug also bit his brother, Gryson Gardner, and the two of them would often be found in their Michigan garage tinkering with various machinery, including drones and electronic kits.

When Gardner arrived at Michigan State, he looked for extracurricular groups and found one dedicated to the increasingly popular hobby of drones. He gained hands-on, practical experience in how drones are made and operated.

In 2021, Gardner received an email from a friend who told him they had just won a USRC grant from NASA for an activity called Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), and they needed help building a new drone.
“We had this idea that instead of flying through the whole city, why can’t a drone just hitchhike a ride on a city bus like everyone else does?” Gardner said.

The concept was for a cargo-carrying drone to take off, dock on top of public transportation such as a bus, charge its batteries while riding along, and then take off for its final leg of the delivery. The team built and flew a full-scale drone to prove the concept but decided against pursuing a commercial venture.

“The commercial drone market kind of scared us a little bit with the large number of regulations that go into operating such a novel idea like this with flying over people in a dense city,” Gardner said.

But the team’s demonstration of technical prowess and confidence led to a second USRC award from NASA in 2023 – the Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS), which focused on using a laser to transfer power directly to a drone in flight.

While working on LEADS, which led to flying a prototype, Gardner’s network of contacts within the drone community expanded to include NASA personnel at the Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, who made him aware of internship opportunities, which he applied for and was accepted while in graduate school.
Gavin Gardner, a University Student Research Challenge participant who went on to co-found his own drone company, also was a NASA intern in 2024 and wrote this social media post.
Student challenge paves way for opportunity

As his graduation in the spring of 2025 with a master’s degree approached, Gardner took the initial steps in late 2024 to co-found with his brother and other USRC alumni AG3 Labs after a friend suggested the military could use low-cost drones to test effective counter drone systems.

An initial award from the U.S. Army led to more contracts, allowing the company to expand and ramp up its operations, where today their production capability enables thousands of drones to be built each month.

Gardner credits his experience with USRC, especially when it came to learning more about the business side of running a technical operation, with helping create the opportunities for success he and his team are experiencing today.

items.title: A soft robot could help doctors diagnose and treat disorders of the small intestine
items.subtitle: MIT engineers designed a robotic enteroscope that can inch through the hard-to-reach small intestine, making biopsies and drug delivery easier.
items.author: Anne Trafton | MIT News
paragraphs: Disorders of the small intestine are often difficult to diagnose and treat. More than 20 feet long, an inch in diameter, and located deep within the body, this organ is harder to access than other parts of the digestive tract, such as the colon or stomach.

To overcome those challenges, MIT engineers have designed a new robotic enteroscope that can move easily through the narrow passage of the small intestine, allowing it to perform imaging, deliver drugs, and remove small polyps or tissue samples for biopsy.

In designing the new robot, the researchers were inspired by the locomotion of snakes, as well as the scaly skin that helps them gain traction on slippery surfaces. A special textured coating helps the robot remain attached to the mucosal lining of the intestine as it inches its way through the narrow tube.
Similar to an endoscope, the robot contains a variety of tools to help detect and treat any abnormalities that it might encounter.
Play video

“When we evaluate the small intestine, we do it for either diagnosis or treatment. If we find a little polyp that needs to be removed, this robot allows us to take a biopsy or remove it,” says Giovanni Traverso, professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, a gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and an associate member of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.

Traverso is the senior author of the study, which appears today in Science Robotics. The paper’s lead authors are former MIT postdoc Binbin Ying, who is now an assistant professor at University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; MIT graduate student Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran; and former MIT research scientist Sahab Babaee.
Snaking through the intestine
The most common problems that doctors need to evaluate within the small intestine include bleeding, lesions, and blockages.

Currently, the only way to diagnose those intestinal complications is with a procedure known as double balloon enteroscopy. During the procedure, an enteroscope advances through the small intestine as a health care worker alternately inflates and deflates two balloons that help propel it through the tract.
This process is slow and laborious, so the MIT team wanted to design an alternative enteroscope that would be easier to control and could move faster through the intestine.
“The fundamental challenge that we’re trying to overcome is how to evaluate that 20-to-25-foot segment of the small intestine in a way that can be more automated,” Traverso says.

The new tube-like robot moves through the narrow small intestine using a locomotion strategy similar to that of the snake. When slithering along the ground, a snake can steer itself by first contracting muscles on one side of the body, then the other.

To mimic this, the researchers designed multifunctional actuators that control the robot’s movement. Each actuator contains four chambers, which can be inflated in different combinations, prompting the tube to extend or bend in any direction.
“By tuning the amount of air that goes into these chambers, you can tune the direction that the robot is moving in,” Traverso says.
The system includes electronics that allow for navigation, with a controller that the person operating the device can use to guide the robot through narrow passages and around tight corners.
Credit: Courtesy of the researchers

The head and tail segments of the robot contain additional expandable anchoring balloons that take turns inflating and deflating, helping the robot move forward. These head and tail segments are coated with special patterned sleeves inspired by kirigami — a variation of origami that involves cutting paper as well as folding it.

Using this technique, the researchers created coatings that lie flat until they are stretched by the expansion of the balloon, which causes three-dimensional kirigami needles to pop out. Similar to the scales of a snake, these needles give the robot more traction within the slippery lining of the intestine.

In previous work, Traverso’s lab has used this approach to create coatings for shoe soles that give them more traction, as well as stents that can temporarily lodge in the esophagus and release drugs.

“By using kirigami sleeves to enhance surface friction, the robot can generate localized tissue engagement traction for locomotion without relying on excessive stretching of the delicate small intestinal tissue,” Jebran says.
Diagnosis and treatment

The system also includes electronics that allow for navigation, with a controller that the person operating the device can use to guide the robot through narrow passages and around tight corners. The soft robot is tethered to the external controllers by a cable and is designed so that it could enter the body through either the mouth or the rectum.
The robot contains tools including a camera for imaging, a sprayer for drug delivery, and clips that can take tissue biopsies or remove polyps.

In animal studies, the researchers showed that the robot could travel about six and a half feet through the small intestine. They also successfully demonstrated the drug sprayer, tissue clips, and camera. The team is now working on improving the navigation systems and testing this approach for additional applications in the small intestine.
“We hope we can continue to move it forward to eventually develop systems that can help achieve more automated evaluation of the small intestine,” Traverso says.

The research was funded, in part, by the Karl van Tassel Career Development Professorship, the MIT Department of Mechanical Engineering, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellowship, an NSERC Postdoctoral Fellowship, the UT Southwestern Medical Center Startup Fund, Samsung Semiconductor and Eurnekian Nanotechnology Graduate Student Fellowships, the Cooke Undergraduate Transfer Scholarship, and the MIT Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program.
